title: Looking for a tech job is a helpless data-entry nightmare
summary:
I spent hundred of hours (distributed over many days) filling my resume data to freshly developed forms made specifically to the hiring process of one or two companies, even though I feel like I have a top 10% resume and years of in hands-down software development experience. I love solving problems, it's part of me.

I know it has got a lot harder to land a development gig but I've worked with modern stuff like AI-generated briefs for meetings, bug logs automatically sent emails to responsible developers, at a point I had an Agent dedicated to verifying how well our code was written so I feel like I've kept up with the innovations, and skills.

But I have no idea how to land a job in software development anymore: nothing seems enough. I have tried for over a year and the only reason I can withstand this much waiting while seeking a job in that field is because of my exceptional employment history (including working to Silicon Valley companies), but it has got to a point I am worried.

I've asked my friends who are also developers and they feel similarly, we do not know where to dedicate our effors, as if the competency of software engineers were transformed irrelevant because of AI. We know what happened, we just don't know what to do with all the competency we embody.

I've taken a liking to working as a bartender in my local city, because that's kind of the only job I can land lately, but as soon as my degree in Computer Engineering is mentioned I'm set aside as a anti-social computer expert who will never take a low-paying job like "this". (Secretly I found it very fun, fullfilling in a way I never thought I needed because money was my priority at the beggining of the carreer)

How the hell do we transform this competency and learning ability of software engineers into desireable company-adding value skills?

(I swear this is not generated by AI, I don't even know how to prove anymore)

title: Ask HN: Why Is Anthropic's Customer Support Bad?
summary:
I've been a Max user of Claude all year and it's crucial to my day to day work. Last night I had a new experience which makes me feel like a junior dev who blew thousands of dollars on a misconfigured AWS CDK file.

To avoid agents doing online research from leaking private info I created a persona which can do online research as a subagent from a fresh context, I asked it to fact check claims as well. Little did I know subagents don't report their token usage and my subagents ended up recursively checking claims. I burned through 80% of my Fable usage for the week in 10 minutes.

I've never come close to using my full token allowance before and now I'm going to have to spend money on expensive usage tokens or upgrade to 20x (or change to a different provider) to complete this weeks work.

Anthropic's online support agent was terse, "empathizing" but ultimately said it could not do anything.

Wouldn't the right thing from a Customer Support perspective to give a one-time usage reset in a case like this? If they had a human instead of an agent doing it, would that have changed the outcome?

I've implemented bounding now in my persona's but it just seems like this is a preventable problem that they're (1) not solving and (2) not willing to remedy when it did happen.

Full disclosure, I love what Anthropic has built in Claude and use the product daily.

Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50252272

title: Reviewing agent output arriving faster than you can inspect it
summary:
It's a curse I know, parallel lanes, context switching. We're told to aim for surgical precision, one item at the time. But when the world is keeping endless inspiration, software commoditised it's hard to live by the rule.

Running several agents at the same time, I found myself having a hard time catching up on everything produced, and giving proper feedback. I tend to actually ask my agent to go through transcripts to find old unfinished tasks and re-state the outputs.

MD files became tedious, screen shots didn't show the entire flow, production code was usually stale or on stuck on a branch.

People out there, do you keep to the rules of capping context switch, or what's the best way to review output here?
